name: Hassan Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good morning, Hassan, and thank you for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good morning. I'll answer straight, but I'll tell you now, I'm not a computer man.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's fine. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a roofing carpenter. I cut and pitch roofs on site, the old way: rafters, purlins, hips and valleys, all measured and cut by hand on a trestle, for a small builder doing houses and extensions round the villages. My father taught me, and his uncle taught him. The best moment is when the last rafter goes in and the shape of the roof is standing there against the sky. The worst is February on a scaffold with frozen fingers, and the trusses, the factory-made roof frames, taking more of our work every year.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Leila works mornings at the bakery on the high street. We have Yusuf, who's thirteen, and Maryam, who's ten. Friday prayers, football on Saturday, my mother for lunch on Sunday. We've got maybe two or three months put by, and the mortgage. I don't use any of the AI. My son tries to show me on his phone and I tell him to put it away at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, of course. A machine can't think like a man who's done a job for twenty-five years. I'd say it at the mosque, at the builders' merchants, to anyone. I don't go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life goes on as it is, and I'm grateful for that. I'd still worry about the trusses taking my work, but that's an old worry, I've lived with it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd go to work, look after my family, keep putting a little by each month. Maybe I'd finally take Yusuf on site in the school holidays, like my father did with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the trusses.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I started, almost every house had a roof cut on site. Now most of the new estates have trusses that turn up on a lorry, already made, and two lads with a crane put the whole roof up in a morning. The extensions and the old houses still need someone like me. That's where my work is now, the odd shapes the factory can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want Yusuf to follow you into the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like it. It's honest work, and it's a skill nobody can take from you. But I'd want him to choose it, not do it because of me. In this world I'd say yes, try it, and see if it's in your hands.

S0.say: Of course a machine can't think like a man who's done a job for twenty-five years. I'd say that at the mosque and the builders' merchants, but I don't go online.
S0.think: It means my life goes on as it is, and I'm grateful. I'd still worry about factory-made trusses taking my work, but that's an old worry I've lived with for years.
S0.do: Carries on working, looking after his family and putting a little aside each month. Thinks about taking his son on site in the school holidays, as his father did with him.
S0.quote: The extensions and the old houses still need someone like me. That's where my work is now, the odd shapes the factory can't do.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan's trade is a family craft, and he has already watched factory-made trusses shrink his work. He is proud and grateful in the plateau picture. Faith and family run through how he describes his life. He doesn't use technology and doesn't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the government should be backing apprenticeships, not computers. If you want people to work, teach them a trade. I'd say it to my local representative if he ever came round, which he doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think more of the odd shapes would go to the factory, because the machines would learn to make them. That's my last corner of the work. I'm not the best roofer in the county. I'm a good one, and good might not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and wait to see what the builder I work for decides. I'd make sure I'm the one he rings first, never late, never a mess. I'd put by a bit more if I could. I wouldn't go on courses for machines, I'd rather do what I know well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a roof that's started to sag a little. You notice it, and you don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your builder brought in a machine and asked you to run it, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let me think about it, and then I'd probably say no. It's not my trade. Let a young man do it. I'd rather find a builder who still wants a roof cut by hand, even if there are fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Karim, he's a bricklayer. And the imam, honestly, he's a sensible man and he's seen a lot of people through bad times. Not the government, they'd send me a leaflet.

S1.say: The government should be backing apprenticeships, not computers. If you want people to work, teach them a trade, and I'd tell my local representative so if he ever came round.
S1.think: More of the odd shapes would go to the factory once the machines learn them, and that's my last corner of the work. I'm a good roofer, not the best, and good might not be enough.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what his builder decides, making sure he's the one the builder rings first. Puts a little more aside if he can and turns down courses on running machines.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like noticing a roof starting to sag.
S1.quote: I'm not the best roofer in the county. I'm a good one, and good might not be enough.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan's public line is about apprenticeships and work, true to his traditional outlook. Privately he admits his skills are solid but not exceptional, and the last corner of his trade is exposed. He'd turn down running a machine. He'd seek advice from his brother and his imam, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's men playing God, the big tech companies, and nobody stopped them. I'd say it at the mosque and to anyone who'd stand still long enough. I'd want someone to put the brakes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd do. That's the truth. Two years, and a robot can cut a roof. I've got two or three months of money, a mortgage, two children, and one skill. I'd feel like a man standing on a roof with the ladder taken away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything, straight away, no meat except on Fridays, no new school shoes until they're worn through. I'd go to my brother Karim and my cousins and see if we could pool together somehow. If it got bad, we'd sell the house and move in with my mother, she's got the room. I don't want handouts, so I'd lean on family and the mosque first, and only take the government's money if there was nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, if I'm honest. I don't panic. But this, yes. I'd not know which way to turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll manage, because that's what a husband says. And she'd look at me and know I didn't know how. She'd probably be the strong one. She'd get more hours at the bakery, and I'd feel ashamed that she had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only take government money if there was nothing else. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I was raised that a man provides. Taking help from your own people is one thing, they know you, you'd do the same for them. Taking a cheque from an office feels like giving up. I know that's pride. But it's how I was made.

S2.say: It's men playing God, the big tech companies, and nobody stopped them. I'd say it at the mosque and to anyone who'd listen, and I'd want someone to put the brakes on.
S2.think: I don't know what I'd do. I've got two or three months of money, a mortgage, two children and one skill, and I'd feel like a man on a roof with the ladder taken away.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone straight away and approaches his brother and cousins about pooling resources. If it gets bad, sells the house and moves the family in with his mother, leaning on family and the mosque before government money.
S2.feel: Panic, which he says is unlike him; he wouldn't know which way to turn.
S2.quote: I'd feel like a man standing on a roof with the ladder taken away.
S2.fieldNote: This picture overwhelms Hassan, with thin savings, one skill and no wish to retrain leaving him without options. He blames tech companies in moral terms. His pride as a provider shapes everything, and he'd turn to family and community before the state. The thought of his wife working more brought out real shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still time to stop this going too far. Put limits on it, keep people in work. And train young men and women in real skills while there's still work to train them for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 48. I'd still not know what I'd do after. But I could get the house in better shape, get some money together, and make sure the children are set on a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every month, as much as I could, maybe 150 extra. I'd pay off the little loan on the van. I'd keep working for as long as there was work, and take every extension and old house job going. I'd talk to Yusuf about not following me into roofing, which would break my heart, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake some nights. Five years sounds long, but it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Yusuf to do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people, maybe a doctor, a teacher. Or something with faith. I don't know if the machines can do those too. If they can, God help us all. I'd tell him to work hard at school, that's all I can say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about your own work in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd do the same work. Maybe I'd ask about teaching at the college, passing on the hand skills. But if nobody's building roofs by hand anymore, who'd want to learn? I'm going round in circles, aren't I.

S3.say: There's still time to stop this going too far: put limits on it, keep people in work, and train young people in real skills while there's still work to train them for.
S3.think: I'd be 48 and still wouldn't know what I'd do after. But I could get the house in order, put money together and make sure the children are set on a path.
S3.do: Saves about 150 extra a month and pays off the small loan on his van. Keeps working and takes every extension and old-house job going, and talks with his son about not following him into roofing.
S3.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep some nights, because five years isn't as long as it sounds.
S3.quote: Five years sounds long, but it isn't.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Hassan time to tidy his finances but no new direction. The idea of steering his son away from the family trade hurt him visibly. He considered teaching the craft, then talked himself out of it and noticed his own circular thinking. He still won't retrain into something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly. Keep families together, give young people apprenticeships, don't just pay people to sit at home. I'd say it to our representative, to the mosque, to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53. That's a long time to keep cutting roofs, and my knees might not last that long anyway. The children would be grown. I could get them through school and maybe into a trade or college before it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep saving, and pay down the mortgage as much as I can. I'd get Maryam and Yusuf through school and help them choose something sensible. I'd still not go on computer courses. If something comes up nearer the time, I'll think about it then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. But less of a weight. Ten years is long enough to sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if something comes up nearer the time. What might that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe building maintenance at the mosque, or some work my brother finds. Maybe the government will have done something by then. I can't plan ten years. I can plan this month, next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Maryam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a teacher. I'd say good, children will always need someone to look at them and say well done. I'd say it as if I'm sure, even if I'm not.

S4.say: Ten years is time to do it properly: keep families together and give young people apprenticeships rather than paying people to sit at home. I'd say it to our representative, the mosque and anyone else.
S4.think: At 53 my knees might not last cutting roofs anyway, and the children would be grown. I could get them through school and into a trade or college before it comes.
S4.do: Keeps working, saving and paying down the mortgage as much as he can. Gets his children through school and helps them choose sensible paths, and still won't take computer courses.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but less of a weight; ten years is long enough to sleep.
S4.quote: I can't plan ten years. I can plan this month, next month.
S4.fieldNote: The decade gives Hassan breathing room mainly through his children growing up first. He doesn't plan a career change and puts off decisions until nearer the time. His values stay steady: work, family and apprenticeships over handouts. He'd show his daughter confidence he doesn't fully feel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have no time and nowhere to go. What would help is if the government made the companies keep people in work, real work, and paid for apprenticeships for the new jobs, whatever they are. Not money for nothing. A way to keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we'd lose. A roof cut by hand lasts a hundred years. My father's roofs are still up. When nobody knows how anymore, that's gone for good. Somebody should care about that, not just the jobs.

headlineQuote: A roof cut by hand lasts a hundred years. My father's roofs are still up.
portrait: Hassan is a 43-year-old roofing carpenter who cuts roofs by hand on houses and extensions, a craft passed down from his father, with a wife who works at a bakery, two children and two or three months of savings. He doesn't use AI and won't train to run machines. He's calm in the plateau picture and uneasy in the steady one, where he admits he's good but not the best. The fast AGI picture leaves him panicked, turning to family and the mosque rather than the state. With more warning time his hope rests on getting his children through school first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no time and nowhere to go with one skill and little savings.
whatWouldHelp: The government making companies keep people in real work and paying for apprenticeships in new jobs, rather than money for nothing.
